summary: Describes the Neighborhood Discovery Protocol for mobile ad hoc networks, which lets a node learn its one-hop and symmetric two-hop neighbors. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Each device on a wireless network shouts hello, hears who is nearby, and learns who the neighbors of its neighbors are.

questions: how does manet neighbor discovery work
what is the nhdp hello message
subtitle: How wireless routers that move around find out who can hear them, and who their neighbors' neighbors are.

tldr.problem: In a mobile ad hoc network, links are lossy, may work in only one direction, and change in seconds as routers move. Routing protocols need to know who is nearby and whether two-way communication really works.
tldr.mechanism: Each router sends HELLO messages on every MANET interface. They carry its own addresses and the status of the neighbors it has heard, so receivers can tell heard links from symmetric ones and learn symmetric 2-hop neighbors.
tldr.outcome: The results are kept in Information Bases that MANET routing protocols can read, for example to pick reduced relay sets. RFC 6130 is a Proposed Standard that has since been updated.

today: RFC 6130 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 7183, RFC 7188 and RFC 7466. Read those together with it.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.content:
RFC 6130 defines the Neighborhood Discovery Protocol (NHDP) for a mobile ad hoc network (MANET). Routers exchange HELLO messages so that each one can find its 1-hop neighbors and its symmetric 2-hop neighbors. Messages are defined and sent in packets according to RFC 5444. The protocol is based on the neighborhood discovery process in the Optimized Link State Routing Protocol (RFC 3626).

The RFC explains why this is harder than in a wired network. Wireless channels are lossy and shared, so if router A can receive from router B, the reverse is not guaranteed. Neighbors may also change on a timescale of seconds, and there is typically no information from lower layers to tell an IP routing protocol about it. A router may also have several interfaces, each with its own channel.

The 1-hop information is for routing protocols that need to know about direct connectivity. The 2-hop symmetric information lets them use flooding reduction, for example by selecting reduced relay sets. NHDP assumes nothing about the link layer except local broadcast or multicast to 1-hop neighbors, and it needs no central entity.
sections.eli5: Imagine a playground where everyone is walking around and shouting, and some kids can hear you but you cannot hear them. This protocol is how each kid works out who can really talk to whom.

sections.title: Neighbors, Links and Symmetry
sections.content:
The RFC builds its vocabulary on a few definitions. A MANET interface of router X is heard by router Y if Y can receive control messages from it. A link exists if either interface can be heard by the other. A symmetric link exists only if both can hear each other.

A 1-hop neighbor is a router whose interface is heard. A symmetric 2-hop neighbor of router Y is a symmetric 1-hop neighbor of a symmetric 1-hop neighbor of Y, other than Y itself. The RFC notes that the 2-hop neighborhood may include routers that are also in the 1-hop neighborhood.

A router needs at least one MANET interface, and each interface has one or more network addresses. Every address must be unique to its router. The same address may be reused on two MANET interfaces of one router only if no MANET interface of another router can communicate with both, for example when they use distinct radio channels.
sections.eli5: Hearing someone is not the same as talking to them. Two kids are real friends only when each one can hear the other, and a friend of a friend is a 2-hop neighbor.

sections.title: The Information Bases
sections.content:
NHDP keeps its state in Information Bases, each made of Protocol Sets that hold Protocol Tuples. An implementation may organize this information differently, as long as it behaves as if tuples were removed at the specified times.

  • The Local Information Base holds the router's own interfaces (the Local Interface Set) and recently used addresses (the Removed Interface Address Set). It is not changed by signaling.
  • Each MANET interface has an Interface Information Base with a Link Set and a 2-Hop Set. A Link Tuple records the neighbor's interface addresses, when the link was last heard and last known symmetric, and a link quality value.
  • The Neighbor Information Base holds the Neighbor Set (all addresses of each 1-hop neighbor, with a symmetric flag) and the Lost Neighbor Set (recently lost symmetric neighbors).

A link's status (PENDING, LOST, SYMMETRIC or HEARD) is worked out in order: PENDING if the link is still a candidate, LOST if it was lost for low quality, SYMMETRIC if its symmetric time has not expired, HEARD if its heard time has not expired, and otherwise LOST. Tuples carry expiry times and are removed when they expire.
sections.eli5: Each device keeps a few notebooks: one about itself, one about each radio it has, and one about its neighbors. Old notes get crossed out when they get too old.

sections.title: The HELLO Message
sections.content:
NHDP defines one message type, HELLO, carried in RFC 5444 packets. HELLO messages must not be forwarded: a msg-hop-limit, if present, must be 1. Every HELLO must contain exactly one VALIDITY_TIME message TLV (from RFC 5497) that says how long its content stays valid. A periodically sent HELLO should also contain exactly one INTERVAL_TIME TLV carrying the sender's HELLO_INTERVAL.

Addresses travel in Address Blocks, and Address Block TLVs give them meaning. LOCAL_IF marks the sender's own addresses, as either the sending interface (THIS_IF) or another interface of the same router (OTHER_IF). LINK_STATUS reports the link status of a neighbor's interface as LOST, SYMMETRIC or HEARD. OTHER_NEIGHB marks an address of a symmetric 1-hop neighbor as SYMMETRIC, or as LOST if it was one recently.

A single address with maximum prefix length (a /32 for IPv4, a /128 for IPv6) on the sending interface may be left out of the Address Blocks if it is the source address of the IP datagram carrying the HELLO.
sections.eli5: A hello message says "this is me, here is how long to trust this, and here is who I can hear and how well."

sections.title: Sending and Processing HELLO Messages
sections.content:
Each MANET interface generates its own HELLO messages. They may be sent at a regular interval (HELLO_INTERVAL), in response to a change in the router or its 1-hop neighborhood, or both. If periodic HELLOs are used, the next must follow within HELLO_INTERVAL, and two successive HELLOs must be at least HELLO_MIN_INTERVAL apart. Jitter as described in RFC 5148 should be used on media where collisions can lose packets.

Every HELLO must contain all addresses of the router's interfaces. Within each REFRESH_INTERVAL, the HELLOs sent on an interface must together report all relevant neighbor information, though that may be split over several messages, for example to fit a small MTU.

On receipt, a router first discards invalid messages silently. Examples include a missing or duplicated VALIDITY_TIME TLV, a hop limit other than 1, a hop count other than 0, and a sender address list that overlaps the receiver's own addresses. Valid messages update, in order, the Neighbor Set, the Lost Neighbor Set, the Link Sets and the 2-Hop Set. A neighbor that reports the receiver's address as heard or symmetric makes the link symmetric. Only when the link is symmetric are the sender's other reported neighbors recorded as symmetric 2-hop neighbors.
sections.eli5: When you hear a hello that mentions you, you know the other kid can hear you too, so the two of you are real friends. Then you write down who their friends are.

sections.title: Link Quality as Link Admission
sections.content:
Some wireless links are marginal. NHDP lets a router record a link quality value in each Link Tuple, a dimensionless number from 0 to 1 where higher is better. It may come from the link layer (for example signal-to-noise ratio), from lost control packets or from lost HELLO messages. Link quality is used only locally and is not sent in signaling, so routers using different or no link quality still interoperate. The RFC stresses that it is a link admission mechanism, not a link metric.

Two thresholds, HYST_ACCEPT and HYST_REJECT, give hysteresis. A link becomes usable when its quality reaches HYST_ACCEPT and is declared LOST when it drops below HYST_REJECT. In between it keeps its previous state, which prevents overly rapid changes. A router that does not use link quality must set INITIAL_PENDING to false and INITIAL_QUALITY to at least HYST_REJECT.
sections.eli5: If a friend's voice keeps cutting in and out, you may decide not to count them as a friend yet. You only change your mind once the voice is clearly good or clearly bad, so you do not flip back and forth.

sections.title: Parameters and Proposed Values
sections.content:
The behavior is tuned by interface parameters and router parameters, which may be set per interface or router and changed at any time within the stated constraints. The main ones are HELLO_INTERVAL (the maximum time between HELLOs), HELLO_MIN_INTERVAL, REFRESH_INTERVAL (the maximum time between reports of each neighbor, never less than HELLO_INTERVAL) and H_HOLD_TIME (carried in the VALIDITY_TIME TLV, at least REFRESH_INTERVAL). L_HOLD_TIME, N_HOLD_TIME and I_HOLD_TIME control how long lost links, lost neighbors and removed local addresses are remembered.

The RFC proposes values for use when a single value of each is wanted: HELLO_INTERVAL of 2 seconds, HELLO_MIN_INTERVAL of HELLO_INTERVAL/4, REFRESH_INTERVAL equal to HELLO_INTERVAL, and H_HOLD_TIME of 3 times REFRESH_INTERVAL. If HELLO messages can be lost, the hold times should be significantly greater than REFRESH_INTERVAL.

Packets may be sent using the "manet" protocol number or the "manet" well-known UDP port, as specified in RFC 5498, and may be sent locally to the link-local multicast address "LL-MANET-Routers".
sections.eli5: There are timers that say how often to shout hello and how long to remember what you heard. The RFC suggests a hello every two seconds and remembering for three times as long as the refresh time.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
If a router sends invalid HELLO messages, whether from malice or malfunction, other routers may record incorrect information. The RFC lists ways a message can be well formed yet wrong: false claims about the sender's own addresses, wrong LINK_STATUS or OTHER_NEIGHB values, and missing or invented neighbor entries. The processing rules keep the Information Bases internally consistent, but the effect of wrong data depends on the protocol that uses them.

The RFC does not give one mechanism for all cases. Some sites control physical access, some link layers already provide authentication, and some uses can tolerate disruption. For other cases it points to the suggestions in RFC 5444 for a cryptographic signature in a message or packet TLV. Because a HELLO's hop limit and hop count are fixed, an end-to-end signature can cover the whole message including its unmodified header. A message that fails verification should be rejected without processing.
sections.eli5: A kid could lie about who they can hear. You can protect yourself with a secret handshake, but in a small, trusted group you might not bother.

items.title: Local Information Base
items.text: The router's own interfaces and recently used addresses. Not changed by signaling.

items.title: Interface Information Base
items.text: One per MANET interface: a Link Set and a 2-Hop Set.

items.title: Neighbor Information Base
items.text: The Neighbor Set and the Lost Neighbor Set for 1-hop neighbors.

items.label: LOCAL_IF
items.desc: THIS_IF = 0 (sending interface) or OTHER_IF = 1 (another interface of the sender).

items.label: LINK_STATUS
items.desc: LOST = 0, SYMMETRIC = 1 or HEARD = 2, for the link from the indicated address.

items.label: OTHER_NEIGHB
items.desc: LOST = 0 or SYMMETRIC = 1, for a symmetric 1-hop neighbor of the sender.
